# Models {#sec-models}

::: {.callout-note}
Revised with assistance from OpenAI Codex/GPT-6 on 2026-09-17.
:::

We estimate distributions of words understood, spoken and signed at monthly ages. These describe both expected counts and the spread around them. A mean alone cannot show how much children differ.

Counts lie between zero and the checklist maximum. We use smooth age functions to describe their distributions while allowing children and studies to differ. These modelling choices express expectations about development; the fitted data and predictive checks determine how well they work.

This section explains Bayesian inference, the model components and the assumptions that affect interpretation.

## Statistical modelling and Bayesian inference

Statistical modelling and inference offer methods for defining mathematical models and fitting them to data to estimate values of interest [@coxPrinciplesStatisticalInference2006; @gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020; @chanStatisticalModelingComputation2025]. They are central to evaluating scientific theories and interpreting data, and can express what a theory means more precisely than words alone [@farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018, chapter 1].

A statistical relationship does not identify its cause. Its interpretation depends on an account of the process being studied and on which alternative explanations the design can distinguish [@spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @vanoijenBayesianCompendium2024; @farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018].

The mapping between the two runs both ways: one empirical model admits many statistical models, and one statistical model is consistent with many empirical models. So even when a statistical model fits the observed data well, we cannot be certain its motivating explanation is 'the right one'; another, equally credible, explanation may fit just as well:

> "Many models correspond to the same hypothesis, and many hypotheses correspond to a single model. This makes strict falsification impossible." [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020, page 4]

Developing and evaluating models is therefore continual and iterative: a competing model may explain the data better, and new observations refine existing models, revise theories and motivate new ones [@gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026].

### Different approaches

There are different approaches to statistical inference, differing in their philosophical and mathematical foundations and in the conclusions they license [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026].

We use Bayesian inference to express uncertainty as distributions, state prior assumptions and predict unobserved outcomes [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026]. These features suit the study's questions. Their usefulness depends on the model assumptions and on checking the resulting estimates.

#### Probability as uncertainty

Bayesian probability expresses uncertainty conditional on stated information [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]. A probability near one assigns high plausibility to an event under the model; a probability near zero assigns low plausibility.

A frequentist confidence interval describes the long-run coverage of a procedure across repeated samples. It does not assign posterior probabilities to values within a particular interval [@moreyFallacyPlacingConfidence2016; @hoekstraRobustMisinterpretationConfidence2014].

#### Estimates as distributions

Bayesian inference begins with a prior distribution for unknown parameters. Bayes' theorem combines it with the likelihood of the observed data to obtain a posterior distribution [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. A posterior interval describes uncertainty about a specified quantity, conditional on that model and those data. It is not automatically a range for individual children.

#### Using existing knowledge

A prior encodes what is plausible about each parameter before the current data are analysed. Priors can draw on previous research and the experience of people with relevant expertise, where this is available. A well-grounded prior combined with the data yields estimates that are more stable, and often more precise, than the data alone. This can be especially valuable when datasets are small or noisy and a substantial evidence base already exists [@gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020].

The need to specify a prior is sometimes criticised as subjective. However, all statistical analyses rest on subjective assumptions [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024, sec. 5; @bergerStatisticalAnalysisIllusion1988; @benjaminRedefineStatisticalSignificance2017; @stuntWhyWeHabitually2021a]. Arguably, Bayesian priors are more explicit and open to scrutiny. A prior "should be chosen, evaluated, and revised just like all of the other components of the model", and we can test directly how sensitive our estimates are to it [@gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. For this study, priors express assumptions about plausible vocabulary trajectories. Sensitivity checks assess how much the reported estimates depend on those assumptions.

#### Predictions for individual children

From the posterior we can predict unobserved outcomes. We draw parameter values and, for a new child, child effects, then simulate an observed count. The resulting *posterior predictive distribution* includes uncertainty about the parameters, differences between children and variation between assessments [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. Its scope depends on which child and study effects are drawn or held fixed.

#### Computation

Modern sampling algorithms approximate posterior distributions that cannot be calculated in closed form [@metropolisEquationStateCalculations1953; @hastingsMonteCarloSampling1970; @hoffmanNoUTurnSamplerAdaptively2014]. Open-source tools such as PyMC implement these methods [@abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023]. Computation can still be difficult, especially when different parameter combinations describe nearly the same data. Sampling diagnostics and model checks are therefore part of the analysis, not optional checks after it.

## Outcomes {#sec-outcomes}

Vocabulary checklists record a subset of the words a child understands, speaks or signs (@sec-data) at a point in time. Each item is a true or false (checked or not checked) option. A child's score is a count of true responses out of $n$ checklist items. One completion of a checklist (an *administration*) yields up to one count per *outcome* (understood, spoken, signed) for a child of a given age. Each such count (one child, one age, one outcome) is an *observation*. We write $W$ for an observed count, subscripted by outcome where the distinction matters: $W_{\text{und}}$, $W_{\text{spkn}}$ and $W_{\text{sign}}$. Our statistical models must consider how observations are distributed.

### A single reference inventory {#sec-reference-inventory}

The pooled checklists differ in length, content and language (@sec-data). We score their raw counts against a common reference of 810 lexical items.[^lexical-items] We do not multiply a count from a shorter form by the ratio of checklist lengths.

[^lexical-items]: A checklist item usually represents a word in one citation form, such as a singular noun or a verb's base form. The score does not count every inflected form separately.

This is an approximation. It assumes that the shorter checklists cover many of the words these children know and that omitted items would add relatively few words at lower counts. A common denominator does not make the inventories identical. Two forms can record the same count from different sets of words, and a child near a short form's ceiling may know many words it does not ask about.

#### Checks on the approximation

We examine proximity to each form's own ceiling, compare raw counts with proportions and fit sensitivities restricted to administrations using the full reference inventory. The restricted fits also change the age and study mix, so they cannot isolate form length perfectly.

The paired DSE and Oxford records provide a further check. Many were taken at different ages. The measurement analysis therefore links each child's assessments while retaining their actual ages, and compares this with same-age and reassigned-age analyses. Read the recorded results and assumptions in the [measurement-analysis script](../../scripts/crosswalk_dse_oxford.py). The evidence can challenge proportional rescaling without proving exact equivalence between forms.

The table below compares typically developing comprehension counts across forms at the same ages. Differences can reflect both the instruments and the studies using them.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

from vocab_growth.report_tables import td_forms_alignment_table, print_small_table

print_small_table(
    td_forms_alignment_table(
        "figures/descriptives/td_form_alignment.csv",
        "figures/descriptives/td_form_alignment_spread.csv",
    ),
    "Words understood reported for typically developing children at 8 to 15 months, by checklist form: the median count as recorded and (in brackets) as a percentage of the form's own item count, with the coefficient of variation (CV) of the form medians on each scale. This compares agreement between form medians on the two scales; it does not establish that the forms measure identical word sets. The Oxford CDI is administered from 12 months.",
    "tbl-td-form-alignment",
)
```

#### Interpretation

Report these estimates as checklist counts on a common reference scale. They are not counts of a child's entire vocabulary. The approximation is especially uncertain near a shorter form's ceiling. Current data checks and native-form sensitivities should accompany any numerical claim about its size; old pool totals do not describe every later fit.

### A Beta-Binomial distribution {#sec-betabinomial}

The words on a checklist are fixed. Therefore, a count $W$ can take only integer values $0 \le W \le n$, and the corresponding proportion $p$ is bounded accordingly. Our outcome model should respect these constraints: counts are discrete, non-negative and bounded above. Since every count in our data is scored against the reference inventory (@sec-reference-inventory), we define $n = 810$.

A count of true responses out of $n$ items follows a Binomial distribution when two assumptions hold within an administration: that (a) given the probability of a true response $p$, the item responses (words checked) are independent; and that (b) every item carries that same probability. This gives a mean of $np$ and a variance (fixed by the mean) of $np(1-p)$ [@gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020, sec. 3.2]. We then assume the same distribution holds across administrations: that (c) the probability is the same for every observation of a given outcome at the same age.

Under the Binomial model, given our inventory of $n = 810$ words, and assuming $p = 0.3$, the expected count would be $np = 243$ with a variance of $np(1-p) = 170.1$, giving a standard deviation of about 13 words. Vocabulary scores vary far more *between* children of the same age than this common probability will allow [@galeoteAcquisitionProductiveVocabulary2008; @marchmanMacArthurBatesCommunicativeDevelopment2023; @zampiniVocabularyDevelopmentChildren2013]. A Beta-Binomial model relaxes assumption (c) by allowing the probability for each observation to vary: rather than one probability shared by all children of an age, each observation's probability is drawn from a Beta distribution [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013, sec. 17.2; @qiaoBetaBinomialModelCount2025].

A Beta-Binomial model also covers departures from assumption (a). Within an administration, responses are unlikely to be truly independent. If one parent completes the whole form, then anything that sways their judgement (for example, a generous or a cautious reading of what counts as "says") sways all the items together. The Beta-Binomial makes no distinction between the two failures: exactly the same distribution of counts arises whether each administration has its own probability or the items within an administration move together, so the two stories cannot be told apart from counts alone. Both are absorbed into the same fitted dispersion.

### What counts retain and lose

Words differ in difficulty and are not equally likely to be known. Under a specific item-response model with known item difficulties and equal discrimination, the total score is sufficient for the child's ability parameter: the particular response pattern adds no information about that parameter once the total is known [@andersenSufficientStatisticsLatent1977; @fischerDerivationsRaschModel1995]. This is a conditional mathematical result. It does not establish that these checklists meet those assumptions, or that a Beta-Binomial count model is equivalent to that item-response model.

Items can differ in how well they distinguish children at different ability levels [@frankVariabilityConsistencyEarly2021, ch. 4; @makranskyItemResponseTheory2016; @kachergisOnlineComputerizedAdaptive2022]. Counts cannot test that assumption or show which words the child knows. They therefore cannot establish that the two populations learn words in the same order. That question needs item-level data.

Unequal item probabilities can also affect count variation. If item responses are independent, the variance of their sum is the Binomial variance at their average probability minus $n$ times the variance of the item probabilities. Unequal difficulty then reduces the variance at a fixed mean. Dependence between item responses can change this result. The Beta-Binomial cannot represent variance below the Binomial floor, so we assess its count predictions against the observations rather than assuming it captures every item-level mechanism.

### The limitations of counts

Equal differences in counts need not represent equal differences in underlying ability. Ten additional words can have different developmental meanings at different ages and starting levels. Counts can still describe change in words, but that change should not be treated as a common ability scale.

Checklist boundaries also limit interpretation. Children who record zero can differ in skills that precede their first words. Children who complete the list can differ in vocabulary beyond it. A percentile adds a comparison with a specified reference group; it does not measure a fixed distance in words or ability. These research samples do not establish population norms.

### The outcome model

For the reasons we have discussed in the preceding sections, we therefore model each count as Beta-Binomial with mean proportion $p$ and concentration $\kappa$:

$$
W \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(n,\,p,\,\kappa),
\qquad
\alpha = p\,\kappa,
\qquad
\beta = (1 - p)\,\kappa,
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the Beta distribution's conventional shape parameters, related to ours by $p = \alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$ and $\kappa = \alpha+\beta$.

Here $p$ is the expected proportion of the checklist that is checked, so the expected count is $\mathrm{E}[W] = np$. The concentration $\kappa$ controls the extra spread. As $\kappa$ grows large the Beta-Binomial approaches the Binomial (less dispersion); as it shrinks, counts spread more widely around the same mean $np$ (more dispersion). This extra variation describes observations around a population trajectory. It should not be confused with uncertainty about the trajectory itself.

Where a model estimates several outcomes jointly (@sec-joint-outcomes), parameters carry the outcome's subscript: $p_{\text{und}}$ is the expected proportion for the count $W_{\text{und}}$, and likewise the concentration $\kappa_{\text{und}}$.

### Age-varying dispersion {#sec-kappa}

For observation $i$ at age $x_i$ months we standardise age,

$$
z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{\sigma_x},
$$

where $\bar{x}$ and $\sigma_x$ are the mean and standard deviation of the ages in the data a model is fitted to, so that $z = 0$ is the average age in that data and one unit of $z$ is $\sigma_x$ months. As a consequence, $z$ means something different in every model, because each is fitted to a different pool of ages: a unit of $z$ spans far fewer months in a model of toddlers than in one spanning childhood. Any prior stated per unit of $z$, such as a slope, therefore expresses a different assumption in months from one model to the next, which is why, wherever we can, we state priors in months (@sec-anchors). Standardising is done to assist computation: the samplers and the Gaussian process approximation (@sec-hsgp) behave better when their inputs are centred near zero and of roughly unit size, and the standardisation itself changes nothing about what a model can express.

Several studies report greater spread in spoken counts at older ages [@berglundParentalReportsSpoken2001; @galeoteDevelopmentVocabularySpanish2011; @marchmanMacArthurBatesCommunicativeDevelopment2023; @zampiniLexicalSyntacticDevelopment2011]. We let concentration vary smoothly with age. Spread in words also depends on the mean and denominator, so a change in count spread does not by itself identify a change in concentration:

$$
\kappa(z) = \kappa_{\min} + \exp\!\left(a_\kappa + b_\kappa z\right).
$$

The exponential term is positive and changes with age; the constant sets a lower bound on concentration. A negative slope makes concentration approach that floor as age increases. A positive slope makes it rise. Neither direction alone determines how the standard deviation in words changes, because the expected count changes too.

The priors on this curve changed partway through the family's development. In the earlier form, the priors sit directly on the three quantities in the formula: the floor $\kappa_{\min}$, the intercept $a_\kappa$, and the size of the slope $b_\kappa$, whose sign is fixed so that the concentration can only fall with age. Two of these are hard to picture. $a_\kappa$ sets the age term at the average age of whatever pool the model is fitted to, so its meaning shifts whenever the pool does, and $b_\kappa$ is a rate of change per $\sigma_x$ months, which shifts with it. In the later form, the curve is the same but the priors sit on quantities that can be pictured and checked: the floor, and how far above the floor the curve sits at two named ages, one young and one old. $a_\kappa$ and $b_\kappa$ are then worked out from those, exactly as the mean trend's intercept and slope are worked out from its two reference ages (@sec-anchors). A prior at a named age can be compared with the data at that age, means the same thing whichever pool of ages the model is fitted to, and leaves the direction of the concentration trend to be decided by the data rather than fixed in advance. Every understood and spoken dispersion curve now uses the later form except in VG05, VG07 and VG08, three development steps that keep the earlier one to remain comparable with the models that descend from them (@sec-model-family); none of the three supplies a reported estimate (@sec-models-of-record), and their dispersion curves are not read as estimates. The signed dispersion curve in VG14 and VG15 also keeps the earlier form, by a separate decision: the registered signing models retain a decreasing-concentration prior. Its adequacy must be checked against their fitted diagnostics and sensitivities.

## Trends {#sec-trends}

The outcome models (@sec-outcomes) give each observation an expected proportion $p$. To investigate how that proportion changes with age, we model a central (mean) trajectory.

Proportions must lie between zero and one, and relating them to age with a straight line ($p = \beta_0 + \beta_1 z$, say) will eventually stray outside those bounds. We therefore build the trajectory on an unconstrained scale: a predictor $f(z)$ of standardised age (@sec-kappa), free to take any value, transformed by the logistic function,

$$
p(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(f(z)\right) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left(-f(z)\right)}.
$$

The logistic function returns a value between zero and one whatever the value of $f$. The inverse of this transformation is the *logit*, $\operatorname{logit}(p) = \log\{p/(1-p)\}$.

Vocabulary development may depart from a straight line on the logit scale. We therefore combine a linear trend with a smooth departure $g$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(z) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 z + g(z),\\
g(z) &= \eta\, g_{\mathrm{unit}}(z), \qquad
g_{\mathrm{unit}} \sim \mathcal{GP}\!\left(0,\, k(\cdot,\cdot)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

### Flexible variations from the central trajectory

The departure $g$ estimates whatever the straight line misses. We do not know the shape of this departure in advance: it might turn upward sharply in the early years, then flatten, or bend more than once. Rather than preselecting a formula (shape), we describe the kind of curve it might be and then let the data pick from that family. That is what a Gaussian process (GP) does [@rasmussenGaussianProcessesMachine2008; @schulzTutorialGaussianProcess2018]. It is a probability distribution over smooth curves, defined not by a formula but by two rules about behaviour: how smoothly the curve may bend, and how far it may stray.

The GP links departures at nearby ages. Data at one age can therefore inform the curve at neighbouring ages. With little nearby evidence, the prior has more influence. The model estimates a distribution of possible curves, so both the fitted departure and its uncertainty matter. A positive departure raises the predicted proportion above the linear trend; a negative departure lowers it.

The length-scale $\ell$ controls how quickly departures can change across ages. Larger values favour slower changes; smaller values allow more rapid changes. The amplitude $\eta$ controls their size on the logit scale.

In the formulas, the rule of resemblance between ages is the kernel $k(z, z')$. We use the radial basis function (exponentiated-quadratic) kernel with its variance fixed at one,

$$
k(z,z') = \exp\!\left(-\frac{(z-z')^2}{2\ell^2}\right),
\qquad k(z,z) = 1,
$$

The amplitude $\eta$ scales the departure, while $\ell$ controls its smoothness. The kernel assigns the same prior correlation to the same age gap throughout the domain. The finite approximation below limits the detail it can represent.

#### HSGP approximation {#sec-hsgp}

A full Gaussian-process calculation can be expensive. A dense covariance calculation relates every observed age to every other, and the cost of that comparison grows with the cube of the number of observations: doubling the data multiplies the work by eight. With several hundred observations per model this would be manageable once, but the sampler must repeat it thousands of times, once for every candidate set of parameter values it tries.

We therefore use the Hilbert-space Gaussian process (HSGP) approximation [@solinHilbertSpaceMethods2020; @riutort-mayolPracticalHilbertSpace2022]. It builds the departure $g_{\mathrm{unit}}$ from a fixed set of smooth waves, from long slow ones to short rapid ones, much as a sound is built from pure tones, and lets the data decide how much of each wave to use. The rules of behaviour are unchanged: the length-scale $\ell$ governs the contribution of faster-varying basis functions, and the amplitude $\eta$ scales the result exactly as before. The parameters keep their meaning, and for a fixed basis size, the main evaluation cost grows approximately in proportion to the number of observations.

Two settings control how faithful the approximation is. The first is the number of waves, $m$. More basis functions can improve the approximation but cost more to fit, and a function allowed to change quickly (a short $\ell$) needs more of them. The second is the width of the age window over which the waves are defined. It must extend some way beyond the ages a model is fitted to, because the approximation deteriorates near its edges, and the boundary factor $c$ sets how far.[^hsgp-domain] The definition and age-grid code determine the units of the length-scale range; inspect their conversion rather than treating every stored bound as months. We choose $m$ and $c$ for that range, following the recommendations implemented in PyMC [@abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023; @riutort-mayolPracticalHilbertSpace2022].

[^hsgp-domain]: The window is centred on the midpoint of the model's declared age domain and extends $c$ times its half-width either side. PyMC's `approx_hsgp_hyperparams` supplies $m$ and $c$ from that domain and the model's length-scale range. Reporting ages are excluded from the domain deliberately, as a presentation choice should not change the fitted model.

### Slope anchors {#sec-anchors}

Rather than placing priors directly on the intercept and slope of the central trajectory ($\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$), we parameterise the linear trend through the expected proportion of words at two reference ages $x_a < x_b$. With $z_a = (x_a - \bar{x})/\sigma_x$ and $z_b = (x_b - \bar{x})/\sigma_x$, and priors placed on $p_{x_a}$ and $p_{x_b}$,

$$
\beta_1 = \frac{\operatorname{logit}(p_{x_b}) - \operatorname{logit}(p_{x_a})}{z_b - z_a},
\qquad
\beta_0 = \operatorname{logit}(p_{x_a}) - \beta_1 z_a .
$$

This gives an interpretable baseline on the logit scale while the GP captures smooth departures.

The reference ages and the priors on $p_{x_a}, p_{x_b}$ are model-specific: 24 and 84 months for the Down syndrome models, 12 and 26 for the typically developing single-outcome models, and 10 and 16 for the young typically developing joint models; 10 and 21 in VG21, whose age window is wider (@sec-model-family). These Beta priors describe the linear trend at the reference ages, not necessarily the complete curve after adding the GP. Their joint implications are checked by prior simulation (@sec-priorpredictive).

## Joint outcomes {#sec-joint-outcomes}

The core structure described in the preceding sections is our starting point, used unchanged by our base models with single outcomes: VG01 (words spoken) and VG02 (words understood) for Down syndrome, and VG03 (words spoken) and VG04 (words understood) for typically developing children. The remaining models estimate two or three outcomes jointly. 

### Production nested within understanding

The joint models assume that spoken words belong to the understood set. They estimate the understood proportion, $p_{\text{und}}(z)=\operatorname{logistic}(f_{\text{und}}(z))$, and the production ratio, the expected fraction of understood words also spoken:

$$
q(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(h(z)\right),
\qquad
p_{\text{spkn}}(z) = p_{\text{und}}(z)\,q(z),
$$

where $f_{\text{und}}$ and $h$ are logit-scale age predictors, each built as in @sec-trends (a linear trend plus a smooth GP departure): $f_{\text{und}}$ carries the age profile of the proportion understood, and $h$ that of the production ratio. Both factors lie between zero and one, so expected spoken vocabulary can never exceed expected understood vocabulary. Subscripts abbreviate the outcomes throughout: $\text{und}$ for words understood, $\text{spkn}$ for words spoken and, from @sec-signed-words, $\text{sign}$ for words signed.

For a usable paired administration, the likelihood first models the understood count out of $n$ items. It then models speech out of that observed understood count, with expected proportion $q$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_{\text{und}} &\sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(n,\, p_{\text{und}},\, \kappa_{\text{und}}\right),\\
W_{\text{spkn}} \mid W_{\text{und}} &\sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(W_{\text{und}},\, q,\, \kappa_{\text{spkn}}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the two steps gives a single, coherent probability for the observed pair, and the constraint $0 \le W_{\text{spkn}} \le W_{\text{und}} \le n$ is respected automatically: the model cannot produce a spoken count exceeding the understood count, because the spoken words are drawn from the understood ones. (The rare recorded pairs that violate the constraint are handled separately, below.) $q$ is therefore a genuine conditional proportion for paired, nested counts, not a ratio imposed on marginal means, and each outcome keeps its own age-varying dispersion (@sec-kappa).

@fig-joint-generative shows this structure. Age shapes spoken vocabulary through two routes: by growing the understood vocabulary from which spoken words are drawn, and by changing the fraction of understood words that are spoken.

![The joint model's generative structure. A paired observation's age determines the expected proportion understood and the production ratio; the understood count is drawn from the full inventory, and the spoken count from the child's understood words. Boxes are observed quantities; rounded nodes are latent ones.](diagrams/fig-joint-generative){#fig-joint-generative width="85%"}

This graph describes the likelihood, not a causal theory of development. Its direction follows the assumed nesting of speech within comprehension. It does not establish whether a change in comprehension causes a change in speech.

Note also the arrow the diagram does not contain: $q$ varies with age but, given age, not with the size of the child's understood vocabulary; the understood count affects the spoken count only as the pool of words the ratio applies to. Two same-age children who understand 100 and 400 words are given the same expected production ratio. Whether the ratio additionally depends on comprehension itself is a question we return to with the cross-lag model (VG16, @sec-child-structure).

### The production ratio $q$ {#sec-production-ratio}

The production ratio $q$ is a composition-weighted average, not an item-level probability. Its definition (the fraction of understood words that are also spoken) might invite reading $q$ as the probability that a given word is spoken once understood; and this would be mistaken. Words differ in difficulty (@sec-betabinomial), and children at a given age understand different numbers of words and different *sets* of words. Therefore, $q$ averages the per-word production probability over whatever vocabulary each contributing child happens to have. Two populations can differ in $q$ purely because their understood vocabularies are composed differently, with no difference in how readily any particular word is produced.[^sufficiency]

[^sufficiency]: Different sets of words can produce the same total. The recorded total alone cannot distinguish those sets, regardless of whether a particular item-response model treats it as sufficient for an ability parameter.

It should also be noted that a contrast at matched comprehension is not a contrast at matched age. Where the report compares Down syndrome and typically-developing children at the same level of comprehension, the groups can differ in age at that matched level. A difference in $q$ read off such a comparison is therefore a difference between groups that are simultaneously unlike in age and in vocabulary composition, and neither can be held fixed while varying the other. Both qualifications apply wherever $q$ is reported.

### Levelling the production ratio's trend above its high anchor {#sec-clamp}

A rising logit-linear production ratio approaches one when extrapolated. At older ages with few paired observations, that behaviour can make the prediction depend mainly on the assumed trend. The Down syndrome joint models therefore flatten the production-ratio trend above its high anchor. They replace age in that linear term with a smooth approximation to its minimum with the high-anchor age:

$$
z_{\text{eff}} = z_b - \frac{1}{s}\operatorname{softplus}\!\big(s\,(z_b - z)\big),
\qquad s = \frac{50}{z_b - z_a},
$$

The transition is smooth rather than a sharp corner. It slightly changes the trend near the high anchor and approaches a flat line beyond it. The GP remains age-dependent, so the full production-ratio curve is not forced to be constant. Its projection uses the same transformed age coordinate.

This rule applies to the production ratio only. It does not flatten the understood trajectory or the single-outcome baselines. The registered signing trend has its own piecewise form, and the typically developing models retain their unflattened trends. These are modelling choices rather than evidence about development outside the reporting window. See the [clamp decision](../../notes/202608141200-clamp-q-only.md) and @sec-models-of-record for reporting limits.

### Signed words {#sec-signed-words}

The signing models add a third outcome and treat it as they treat speech: a signed word is one of the words the child understands. Alongside the production ratio they estimate a *sign ratio* $r$, the expected fraction of understood words that the child also signs,

$$
r(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(f_{\text{sign}}(z)\right),
\qquad
p_{\text{sign}}(z) = p_{\text{und}}(z)\,r(z),
$$

and score a signed count against the child's understood count, exactly as the spoken count is scored:

$$
W_{\text{sign}} \mid W_{\text{und}} \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(W_{\text{und}},\, r,\, \kappa_{\text{sign}}\right).
$$

Signed vocabulary can therefore never exceed understood vocabulary, and $r$ carries the same qualifications as $q$: it averages over whatever words each child happens to understand, and is not the probability that any particular word is signed (@sec-production-ratio). The registered signing models use only Down syndrome observations; one of them defines its column to include spontaneous symbolic gestures alongside taught signs (@sec-data).

@fig-signing-generative extends @fig-joint-generative with the third outcome: the signed count is drawn from the child's understood words exactly as the spoken count is, each through its own ratio.

![The signing models' generative structure. Age determines the expected proportion understood, the production ratio and the sign ratio; the understood count is drawn from the full inventory, and the spoken and signed counts are each drawn from the child's understood words. Boxes are observed quantities; rounded nodes are latent ones.](diagrams/fig-signing-generative){#fig-signing-generative width="85%"}

Signing can follow a different course from speech. A small longitudinal study observed transitions from signs to speech in some children [@kaat-vandenosExpressiveVocabularyDevelopment2017]. This motivates allowing a rise and fall, but does not establish a preschool peak for the population. The model expresses this possibility in its prior trend. Its prior is centred on zero departure at every age, so with a flat trend the prior would say that signing is equally common at every age, and the data would have to build the whole hill unaided. $f_{\text{sign}}$ therefore replaces the single straight line with a *tent*: priors on the ratio at three reference ages, 15, 36 and 96 months, joined by straight lines on the logit scale, with priors favouring a rise and fall, and a trend that is flat beyond the outer two. The anchor values are not constrained to make the middle one the largest. The GP adds smooth departures as before. VG14 fixes the middle reference age at 36 months. VG15 estimates its position between the outer ages. Neither this position nor the peak of the trend must equal the peak of the complete signed-count curve after the GP and comprehension trajectory are included.

As with the other trends, the GP is stripped of anything the tent itself could express (@sec-gpanchor), so the three reference levels keep their meaning. Even so, the signed trajectory leans on its parametric shape more heavily than the other outcomes lean on theirs. Signed observations are dense from about 12 to 60 months and thin beyond, the outer reference ages are asserted rather than fitted, and the GP's length-scale is only weakly identified, so at older ages the curve is shaped more by the prior than by the data. Whether signing and speaking cluster on the same words is a separate question, taken up next (@sec-speech-sign-association).

### The sign--speech association {#sec-speech-sign-association}

VG14 assumes that, within the understood set, signing and speaking a word are independent at a given age. It derives total expressive vocabulary, the union of the two modalities, under that assumption. It does not estimate their overlap from cross-tabulated data.

VG15 estimates the association instead, because four pooled sources record production word by word in both modalities and so carry more than marginal counts. uk_02 and uk_07 record, for each understood word, whether the child signs it, says it, does both or neither. es_01 records totals from which the same four cells follow by subtraction, with the caveat that its non-vocal column is defined to include spontaneous symbolic gestures alongside taught signs and may cover only ten of its form's 21 word categories (@sec-data). nz_01 records, within produced words, whether each is spoken, signed or both. These compositions are scored with a Dirichlet-Multinomial term in place of the separate spoken and signed likelihood contributions; each composition is conditional on its observed total, so the understood likelihood is unchanged. The association is carried by a Plackett odds ratio $\psi$: among the words a child understands, the factor by which being signed multiplies the odds of also being spoken. $\psi = 1$ recovers VG14's independence; $\psi > 1$ means signing and speaking cluster on the same words.

@fig-sign-speech-composition shows how this changes the structure of @fig-signing-generative. Among the words a child understands, each is neither spoken nor signed, spoken only, signed only, or both. The composition is observed for the four word-level sources and latent elsewhere, where only its margins, the spoken and signed counts, enter the likelihood; $\psi$ couples the two modalities within it. Setting $\psi=1$ gives independent sign and speech probabilities within a word. It does not make VG15's Dirichlet-Multinomial composition likelihood identical to VG14's separate Beta-Binomial likelihoods.

![How VG15 scores production in both modalities. Among the words a child understands, each is neither spoken nor signed, spoken only, signed only, or both. The composition (dashed) is observed for the four sources that record production word by word and latent elsewhere, where only its margins enter. The association $\psi$ (dashed) couples the two modalities within understood words; setting it to one gives independent sign and speech probabilities within a word, while the composition likelihood remains distinct from VG14's separate count likelihoods. Boxes are observed quantities; rounded nodes are latent ones.](diagrams/fig-sign-speech-composition){#fig-sign-speech-composition width="85%"}

The association $\psi$ varies by study. In the recorded analysis, age alone did not explain the study differences, and adding age after study gave no clear improvement. This does not rule out every age effect. With four informing sources, the between-study spread is weakly identified and sensitive to its prior. Read study-specific estimates alongside the pooled centre. @sec-data describes the source fields and masking rules.

### When only one count of a pair is recorded

When the understood count is unavailable, the spoken or signed count remains usable through a marginal fallback,

$$
W_{\text{spkn}} \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(n,\, p_{\text{und}}\,q,\, \kappa_{\text{spkn}}\right),
$$

and analogously for signing. The observation builder can also route a non-nested recorded pair to this fallback. The default loader masks comprehension contradicted by recorded spoken or produced counts before graph construction; reinstatement sensitivities can exercise the violation path.

The fallback reuses the conditional branch's dispersion $\kappa_{\text{spkn}}$, and that is an approximation: on conditional rows the dispersion is variation in $q$ alone, whereas fallback rows also absorb unobserved variation in $p_{\text{und}}$. One variance comparison can be derived exactly at fixed model parameters: the true marginal of a fallback row is more dispersed than the fallback's Beta-Binomial precisely when $q\,\kappa_{\text{spkn}} > \kappa_{\text{und}}$; the level $p_{\text{und}}$ drops out entirely; and the two variances are equal on the boundary.[^fallback-moments] The fallback is therefore neither conservative nor anti-conservative as a structural matter: which way a given model errs is a question about its fitted concentrations. Three registered sensitivity analyses assess its effect: dropping the fallback rows altogether, giving the fallback branch its own dispersion through a single signed scalar that nests the default at zero, and replacing the fallback's dispersion with the one matching the true marginal's first two moments; and posterior-predictive calibration is reported separately for the conditional and fallback rows, which differ systematically in age and study composition.

[^fallback-moments]: Binomial thinning collapses the paired factorisation to $W_{\text{spkn}} \mid \theta_{\text{und}}, \theta_{\text{spkn}} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}\!\left(n,\, \theta_{\text{und}}\theta_{\text{spkn}}\right)$, so the true marginal of a fallback row is a Binomial mixed over the *product* of two independent Beta variates. That product is not itself Beta, but both its moments are elementary, and comparing them with the fallback's reduces to the single condition given here.

## Multilevel models {#sec-randomeffects}

The observations are not independent of one another, in two ways. Many children are measured more than once, so their administrations share whatever makes that child unusual. And every administration comes from one of the pooled studies, which differ in instrument, recruitment, language and country, so administrations from the same study share whatever makes that study unusual. Treating the rows as independent would let a large study's level pass for the population's, and would overstate how precisely the curves are known.

The multilevel models therefore give each study and each child its own offset from the population curve. For a predictor $f_\bullet$, standing for $f_{\text{und}}$, $h$ or $f_{\text{sign}}$, the offsets enter on the logit scale,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_\bullet(z_i) &\;\to\; f_\bullet(z_i) + \delta^{\text{study}}_{\bullet,\,s(i)} + \delta^{\text{subj}}_{\bullet,\,j(i)},\\
\delta^{\text{study}}_{\bullet} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}\!\left(0,\, \tau^{\text{study}}_\bullet\right),
\qquad \tau^{\text{study}}_\bullet \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(0.5),\\
\delta^{\text{subj}}_{\bullet} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}\!\left(0,\, \tau^{\text{subj}}_\bullet\right),
\qquad \tau^{\text{subj}}_\bullet \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(1.5),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $s(i)$ and $j(i)$ are the study and child of observation $i$.[^non-centred] The offsets are not fitted freely. Each set is drawn from a Normal distribution centred on zero whose spread $\tau$ is estimated from the data, so a study or child with little data is pulled toward the population curve, and one with much data can stand apart from it. The study offsets are constrained to sum to zero, so the population curve is the curve of an average study rather than of any particular one. An offset shifts a curve up or down on the logit scale and nothing else: studies and children are assumed to differ in level, not in shape, an assumption the child-level models of @sec-child-structure relax for children.

[^non-centred]: The offsets are sampled in the non-centred form, as a unit-scale draw multiplied by $\tau$, which changes the sampler's coordinates and nothing about the model. VG11 and VG12 sample their study offsets in the centred form instead, because each of their datasets carries thousands of administrations and the trade-off reverses.

The two spreads have different priors because the data put them on different scales. Fitted outside the models with the same grouping structure, children of the same age in the same study differ with a standard deviation of 0.74 to 1.15 logits across the family, roughly the difference between understanding 300 and 500 of the 810 words at the same age, while studies differ by about a third of that. The child prior has its median near one logit and the study prior is correspondingly tighter. With child offsets in the model, the Beta-Binomial dispersion of @sec-kappa describes the scatter of a child's administrations around that child's own curve, and the child offsets describe the scatter of children around the population curve.

**The reported population curves set every offset to zero.** They describe a reference child in a zero-offset study, and a study's or a child's own curve is that curve shifted by its offset. Predictions are reported in two forms (@sec-interval-convention). A population-level predictive interval keeps the offsets at zero, so it carries uncertainty about the curve and the scatter of administrations around it. A subject-marginal predictive interval also draws a fresh child offset from the fitted spread; it answers where one more child would fall, and usually gives a wider interval. Both forms still condition on the stated treatment of study effects.

In the Down syndrome family, VG07 adds the study offsets to VG05, VG08 and VG09 add child offsets on the proportion understood and then on the production ratio, and VG10 and every model derived from it carry both, as does VG15. The typically developing hierarchical models, VG11 to VG13, carry a dataset offset and a child offset, on their single outcome in VG11 and VG12 and on both the proportion understood and the production ratio in VG13. They exclude Wordbank datasets contributing fewer than 200 administrations, whose offsets would be barely identified, and because many Wordbank children appear only once, their child spread is identified mainly by the children measured more than once. A sensitivity analysis for these models keeps one randomly chosen administration per child, with a fixed seed, and drops the child offsets, as a check that conclusions do not depend on how repeat administrations are treated.

### Anchoring the smooth departure {#sec-gpanchor}

Child offsets create a problem the single-level models do not have. Suppose the whole population's curve sat a little higher. The model could now write that in three places: in the trend's intercept, as a constant lift in the smooth departure $g$, or spread across every child's offset.[^study-sum] Every combination of the three that adds up to the same lift fits the data identically, so the data cannot choose between them, and the sampler has to explore all of the equivalent combinations rather than settle on one. In the models with child offsets on both the proportion understood and the production ratio this made sampling slow and unreliable: the trend's parameters became correlated in the posterior with the departure's amplitude and length-scale, and those models had the worst convergence diagnostics in the family.

[^study-sum]: The study offsets cannot carry it, because they are constrained to sum to zero (@sec-randomeffects).

The remedy is to pin the departure. In the anchored models two rules hold in every posterior draw. First, $g$ is exactly zero at a reference age, always the midpoint of the model's two anchor ages: 54 months for the Down syndrome models, 19 for VG11 and VG12, 13 for VG13 and VG23, and 15.5 for VG21. Second, any straight-line component of $g$ across the observed ages is removed and left to the trend.[^anchor-rows] The trend then owns the level and the slope, the offsets own the shifts of studies and children, and the departure owns only the bends. This assigns different roles to the trend and smooth departure. The projection changes the prior on the complete function; it is not merely a change of sampling coordinates. Comparisons must check its effect on fitted trajectories.

[^anchor-rows]: The straight-line component is computed from the observed administrations only, so the ages at which the report asks for predictions cannot affect the fit. Where the production ratio's trend is levelled above its high anchor, the component removed is the levelled line, so the two devices agree (@sec-clamp). In VG15 the signing ratio's departure is treated the same way against its three-anchor tent.

VG10 is VG09 with this device and no other change, introduced when child offsets on the production ratio exposed the problem. VG15, VG16 and the typically developing multilevel models carry it for the same reason, and every model derived from VG10 or VG13 inherits it. The earlier development steps, VG05, VG07 to VG09 and VG14, predate it and are kept as they were, because the one-change-at-a-time ladder is what shows what the device contributes.

## Sex {#sec-sex-covariate}

<!--
Section drafted by an LLM-based AI tool (Claude Code/Opus 5), 2026-09-13, for
the sex covariate the reporting models carry from that date (issue #324). The
evidence figures are from notes/202609041206-sex-differences-in-vocabulary.md.
-->

Girls and boys of the same age differ a little in the vocabulary their parents report. Before any model carried sex, regressions fitted outside the models found girls ahead by about 0.2 logits on words understood and about 0.35 on words spoken, of similar size in the Down syndrome and typically developing pools, with no detectable change in the difference with age on the logit scale; against the models' own child spreads that is about 1% of the variation between children. It is small beside how much children differ, but large enough to change the typical count quoted for a child, and the typically developing norms for these checklists are published separately for girls and boys for that reason.

The models whose numbers are reported (@sec-models-of-record) therefore carry sex as a covariate; the development steps do not. Each child $j$ has $x_j = +\tfrac{1}{2}$ for a girl, $x_j = -\tfrac{1}{2}$ for a boy and $x_j = 0$ where sex is not recorded, and it enters each trajectory's predictor on the logit scale beside the offsets above,

$$
f_\bullet(z_i) \;\to\; f_\bullet(z_i) + \delta^{\text{study}}_{\bullet,\,s(i)} + \delta^{\text{subj}}_{\bullet,\,j(i)} + \beta^{\text{sex}}_\bullet\, x_{j(i)},
\qquad \beta^{\text{sex}}_\bullet \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\, 0.5),
$$

so $\beta^{\text{sex}}_\bullet$ is the difference between girls and boys in logits, the same at every age. A constant logit difference gives a count difference that depends on the starting probability and denominator. It can grow and then shrink as probabilities approach their bounds.

**No administration is dropped for want of a recorded sex.** In the Down syndrome pool sex is recorded by whole studies: eight of the fifteen record it for every child and seven for none. A child of unrecorded sex sits at the midpoint between girls and boys, and the study offsets can account for some differences in study composition. This does not recover the missing sex of an individual child. The common sex coefficient is learned from recorded sex and assumed to apply to studies without it. In the typically developing data sex is missing only for VG11, for about 5% of its children, nearly all of them in the one dataset that records none; study offsets again permit study-level differences, while assigning missing sex to the midpoint remains an assumption to assess. In VG15 and the models built on it, the coefficients also enter the word-level compositions of @sec-speech-sign-association, unlike the child offsets, so $\psi$ describes the association for a child of given sex.

**The reported population curves are drawn at the midpoint**, on the logit scale. This reference is not generally the arithmetic average of girls' and boys' expected counts, and each model's technical report gives girls' and boys' expected counts either side of them, with single-child ranges where the model draws a new child.

## Child-level structure {#sec-child-structure}

A child's offset in the multilevel models is a single constant per trajectory, and that carries two restrictions. Every child's curve is parallel to the reference curve on the logit scale. The gap in words can still change, but the model cannot represent a changing child-specific logit offset. And a child's offsets on different trajectories are drawn independently, so knowing that a child understands more than most says nothing about whether they say more of what they understand. Neither restriction is innocent, and the models in this section relax them one at a time. VG20, and its typically developing counterpart VG23, relax the second; VG19 relaxes the first; VG22 relaxes both together. Each is a refinement of VG10 or VG13 that contains its parent as a special case, so the data are free to answer 'no change'. VG16 is different in kind: it extends VG09 with a predictor rather than a random effect, and asks a different question.

### Correlated child effects

VG10 draws comprehension and production-ratio child offsets independently. VG20 estimates their correlation $\rho_{uq}$ under a prior centred on zero.[^lkj] The independence structure is recovered at $\rho_{uq}=0$. VG20 also carries the sex covariate absent from VG10, so a fit comparison does not isolate correlation alone. Refitting can change both child predictions and reference curves.

[^lkj]: An LKJ prior with $\eta = 2$, which for two effects places a $\mathrm{Beta}(2, 2)$ distribution on $(\rho_{uq} + 1)/2$.

VG23 adds a correlated child block and sex effects to VG13. Paired comprehension and speech observations can inform the association, but separating persistent child variation from residual variation remains difficult when few children are seen twice. The same parent reports both counts, and neither model separates informant effects from child differences. Recovery and prior sensitivity checks are needed; an apparent bias in another model does not supply a bound on the truth.

### Child slopes

VG19 allows a child's logit offset to change with age. The offset is $b_0+b_1(a-36)/12$, where $b_0$ is the level at 36 months and $b_1$ the yearly change. Centring age can reduce dependence between these estimates but does not guarantee independence. Each trajectory has a jointly drawn level and rate. VG10 is the special case with no variation in rates.

The child-slope design followed a comparison of constant offsets, linear change and temporary deviations on VG10 residuals. The [design record](../../notes/202608141900-child-slope-implementation-plan.md) preserves that evidence and its limits. Both comprehension and production-ratio terms can affect spoken change, so a spoken trajectory alone cannot identify which term explains it.



VG20 correlates comprehension and production-ratio levels. VG19 correlates each trajectory's level with its rate. A joint model of all four effects needs six pairwise correlations, including relationships between rates. VG22 addresses that wider structure.

### A low-rank factor

**VG22** links all four child effects, level and rate on each trajectory, in one structure. Rather than estimating a free covariance among the four, it supposes that each child's four effects are combinations of a smaller number $k$ of underlying scores: $b = Lz$, with $z$ the child's $k$ standard normal scores and $L$ a $4 \times k$ matrix of loadings shared by all children. This guarantees a valid covariance by construction, and the number of underlying dimensions, the rank $k$, is the model's one structural choice.

Exploratory residual fits motivated a reduced-rank structure. The registered VG22 uses rank three, with rank-one and rank-two sensitivities. These ranks can differ in their implied rate magnitudes. The [resolved reporting gate](../../notes/202609091200-vg20-vg22-gate-resolved.md) explains why VG22 remains a development model.

The four spreads keep the names, priors and meanings they have in VG19 and VG20, and the level-level correlation $\rho_{uq}$ is given the same prior VG20 places on it, built deliberately into the loading structure rather than left to whatever distribution that structure would otherwise induce. The two models therefore estimate the shared quantity under the same prior, and a difference is not explained by different marginal priors on that correlation alone. The surrounding covariance structures and joint priors still differ. VG19, by contrast, is not a special case of VG22 at any rank below four, so that comparison is between two models rather than within one.

### The cross-lag

The joint models make the production ratio a function of age alone: given age, how much a child understands affects the expected spoken count only through the pool of understood words the ratio applies to (@sec-joint-outcomes). **VG16** asks whether a child's comprehension history shifts the ratio itself. For each administration with an earlier one from the same child, the previous understood count, expressed as a deviation from the population curve at that age, enters the current production ratio with a coefficient $\beta_{\text{lag}}$ under a prior centred on zero, so that neither direction is imposed.[^wave] The estimate needs careful reading. Because a deviation from the population curve retains each child's persistent standing, $\beta_{\text{lag}}$ mixes a between-child association; children who understand more also say more of it; with a within-child one, and it is not evidence of a temporal direction. VG16 exists to estimate this single quantity and supplies no other reported number. Its estimate is currently withdrawn: the construction of the lag was corrected after review, and no figure will be reported until the corrected model has passed a reporting-quality fit (@sec-models-of-record).

[^wave]: An administration wave contains all rows for a child at one recorded age. Rows in the same wave receive the same earlier source, so the predictor does not depend on input row order.

The gaps in the numbering are deliberate. VG06, the original typically developing joint model, was retired outright when the instrument supplying most of its comprehension rows proved to record comprehension as a proxy for production; VG13 replaced rather than repaired it. VG17 and VG18 are reserved for exploratory, unregistered prototypes that bypass the validation machinery below (@sec-estimation); their output is not validatable and none of it is published.

The main DS sequence adds study effects, child effects and GP anchoring from VG05 through VG10. VG19, VG20 and VG22 extend its child structure. The signing sequence runs from VG14 through VG15 to VG24 and VG25. On the TD side, VG11 and VG12 are single-outcome references; VG13, VG21, VG23 and VG26 are joint models. Each model report documents its priors, diagnostics, sensitivities and fitted summaries.

# Estimation and validation {#sec-estimation}

## The iterative workflow

We follow the iterative Bayesian workflow described by @gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020: specify a transparent model, simulate from its priors, fit it, inspect computation and predictive behaviour, identify a concrete inadequacy, and only then add structure. The numbered models preserve that development history. A later number is not automatically better: an extension must solve a named problem and survive the same checks as its predecessor, and @sec-models-of-record records which models currently carry reported numbers.

## The fitting pipeline

Models are defined in PyMC and sampled with the NUTS sampler [@abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023; @hoffmanNoUTurnSamplerAdaptively2014]. Every registered model runs the same ordered pipeline: prepare data; construct priors; build the model; prior predictive checks; sampling; convergence diagnostics; posterior predictive checks; posterior summaries, plots and the model report. The standard sampling configurations are `dev`, `test` and `rep`, with named overrides for specific runs, and only reporting-quality fits can source a numerical claim in this report. Each fit is written to an isolated staging area and promoted atomically only after the statistical pipeline succeeds, so a failed or interrupted run can never overwrite a good fit, and report rendering runs afterwards as a separate, retryable step.

## Prior predictive checks {#sec-priorpredictive}

Before the models see the study outcomes, we draw trajectories and replicated scores from the priors alone. We require bounded scores, plausible levels at the youngest and oldest relevant ages, developmental change that is smooth on a realistic time scale, and enough dispersion to represent heterogeneous children without placing substantial probability on implausible extremes. A prior predictive failure is addressed by revising the assumptions or their parameterisation; with any use of these data to inform a revision disclosed. Data-informed calibration is not independent prior evidence.

## Convergence diagnostics {#sec-convergence}

Reporting fits are checked for R-hat no greater than 1.01 and bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least 400 on the quantities selected for the diagnostic scan [@vehtariRankNormalizationFolding2021]. These are screening rules, not proof that sampling found every relevant part of the posterior. A hard-gate failure prevents promotion to a completed reporting fit.

A study-owner-approved exception can permit a named parameter to exceed the R-hat threshold up to a recorded ceiling. It does not excuse an effective-sample-size shortfall. The current VG11 entry covers the GP length scale and one basis coefficient; the [2026-09-16 decision](../../notes/202609160500-vg11-length-scale-exception.md) records the evidence and limit. Use the fit's diagnostic record to see whether the exception was actually needed.

Divergent transitions and energy BFMI below 0.3 are recorded as caveats. They can affect estimates as well as interval bounds, so disclosure does not establish that every quantity is reliable. Publication requires the applicable validation policy and an explicit account of unresolved problems.

## Posterior predictive checks and calibration {#sec-predictive-calibration}

Posterior predictive checks generate replicated outcomes from the fitted model and compare them with the observations: distributional overlays, bounded-count behaviour across age and, for the joint models, the paired outcomes together, fallback rows included; the signing model additionally checks the sign-by-speech cells that identify $\psi$. Alongside the visual checks, every fit writes a numerical calibration table recording, for each outcome, overall and within age bands, the mean observed and predicted counts, the empirical coverage of the predictive interval at its stated width, and the distribution of the probability integral transform; each observation's position within its own predictive distribution. Coverage near nominal and a near-uniform transform indicate a predictive distribution that is neither too wide nor overconfident, and departures are directional, so the table says not only whether but how a model misfits. These checks are in-sample; the replications condition on parameters the same observations informed; so their value is comparative, across models, outcomes and ages, and gross misfit is what they catch first; the out-of-sample counterpart is the comparison standard below (@sec-supersedes). A model can pass every sampler diagnostic and fail these checks: convergence shows that computation characterised the specified posterior, not that the specification represents the data.

## Parameter recovery

For the models that carry reported numbers, we simulate data from the model at known parameter values, refit the model to the simulation with the same pipeline, and score the recovered posterior against the truth. A replicate counts only if its own fit converges. A small study can reveal large errors worth investigating at the tested truths. It cannot estimate interval coverage precisely or establish identification over the full parameter space.

## Sensitivity analyses

Where a defensible alternative exists to a data rule, a prior or a structural choice, it is registered as a named variant and fitted with the same pipeline rather than argued about: each masked data-defect class has a reinstatement variant, the priors that carry real weight have widened counterparts, the young typically developing window has alternative widths, and the fallback likelihood has three registered alternatives (@sec-joint-outcomes). A variant's fit is compared with the baseline quantity by quantity against the baseline's own posterior intervals, so a robustness claim in this report is a measurement, not an impression.

## Model comparison, and what 'supersedes' means {#sec-supersedes}

A reporting role requires a recorded decision based on the model's purpose and evidence, including structural checks, predictive performance and uncertainty. A model of record supplies specified results; a TD reference supplies a comparison; a development step supports evaluation. Registration or a higher model number alone assigns no reporting role.

## Reporting conventions {#sec-interval-convention}

The usual summaries are the posterior median and inner 50% and outer 89% intervals [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. Intervals are equal-tailed by default. Selected skewed or boundary-censored quantities use highest-density intervals, including association, concentration and some milestone summaries. Read each output's `interval_kind` rather than assuming one convention applies everywhere. Density plots show features that intervals can hide.

Several estimands rest on modest samples, and a point estimate selected for looking decisive is on average inflated in magnitude and can even take the wrong sign; the Type-M and Type-S errors that follow from selecting on a noisy estimate. We therefore lead with the interval and the strength of evidence for a named claim, and treat the point estimate as the least informative summary.

**Reference-trajectory intervals** describe uncertainty in the age curve with study and child effects set to zero. **Reference predictive intervals** also include residual count variation at those zero effects. **New-child predictive intervals** additionally draw child effects while retaining the stated study reference. These describe different quantities and are not population norms. A reference curve's crossing age is also different from the distribution of individual children's milestone ages.

## Provenance

Every fit records a manifest carrying the complete model definition, the sampling configuration, fingerprints of the raw inputs, an exact hash of the prepared analysis data, and the code revision and environment that produced it. Before any figure or table reaches this report, the fit behind it is re-validated field by field against the current definitions and data rules, so a posterior that predates a change to either is identified as stale and cannot be republished silently. The same checks gate the model-comparison outputs, and each model's technical report carries its per-fit diagnostic record.

## Models of record {#sec-models-of-record}

Which model supplies each reported estimate is a recorded decision under the taxonomy of @sec-supersedes, reviewed whenever a model is added or a defect is found; never an implication of the numbering. Between them, the current assignments cover the study's aims (@sec-intro): the Down syndrome trajectories, ranges and milestone summaries, and the contrasts with typically developing children.

### Words understood

The Down syndrome comprehension estimates come from **VG20**, the joint model of record. It replaced VG10 in August 2026, when VG10's assumption of independent child effects was contradicted by its own fitted deviations; the population trajectories are reproduced essentially unchanged, so the succession supersedes VG10's child-level intervals rather than withdrawing its curves. Down syndrome comprehension quantities are reported to 72 months: the 72–84-month band is populated, but the candidate child structures disagree there by most of an interval width while remaining indistinguishable out of sample, so a number in that band would reflect the model choice more than the data. The typically developing comprehension reference is **VG12**, reported to 25 months, where its pool's comprehension observations stop.

### Words spoken

VG20 supplies DS spoken estimates to 90 months. VG11 supplies the TD spoken reference. VG21 supplies the TD joint comparison at matched comprehension over 8–22 months, replacing VG13 in that role. VG23 supplies the TD child-effect correlation over its shorter 8–18-month window.

### Words signed or gestured

VG15 supplies signed trajectories, the within-word sign–speech association and total expressive vocabulary. VG24 supplies the between-child signed-share/spoken-share correlation, `rho_sign_q`. VG14 remains a development baseline. It differs from VG15 in more than the independence assumption, so their full-fit difference is not solely the cost of independence.

### The rest of the family

VG01–VG05, VG07–VG10, VG14, VG16, VG19 and VG22 are development models. VG13 is superseded for matched-comprehension reporting. VG25 and VG26 remain unclassified candidates. The [model inventory](../models/README.md) records the current roles and links to the decisions. Update the inventory, catalogue and affected reports together when a role changes.
